Managing Trust Relationships | SAP Help Portal

Required for SSL connections using the Secure Socket Layer, SAPSSLS.pse is installed automatically and is available by default.

entry.title: Batch transfers in SAP B1 without selecting every batch
entry.content:
Environment: SAP Business One 10, Service Layer, SQL Server / HANA

Introduction

Moving batch-managed stock between warehouses in SAP Business One means selecting batches by hand for every line, which gets slow when items have many batches. This post shows how to prepare the whole transfer in one Excel sheet and post it through the Service Layer as a single document.

The problem

While working on an SAP project, I noticed how slow it is to move batch-managed stock between warehouses. Many items have several batches. In the Inventory Transfer window you have to open the batch selection and pick the batches for each line, one by one. DTW doesn’t make it easier, because the batch lines go in a separate file. Either way it takes hours, so I looked for a faster way.

The approach

The idea is to keep everything in one Excel sheet, with one row per item and batch. The columns the transfer needs are the item code, the batch number, the quantity to move, the source warehouse and the destination warehouse.

  1. Export the batches that have available stock. The export has the item code, batch number, quantities and the warehouse they are in. On SQL Server this is a read-only query. On HANA, I run a saved query inside B1 and export the result.
  2. Add two columns: Transfer Qty and To Whs.
  3. Fill them in only for the rows you want to move.
Item No.Batch NumberFrom WhsTo WhsTransfer Qty
ITEM2001BT101W8121
ITEM2001BT201W8122
ITEM2001BT301W812 3

The sheet can hold as many items as you need, and they all go into one document. Rows are grouped by item code, from-warehouse and to-warehouse. Each group becomes one line of the transfer, with its batches inside. Rows where both warehouses are the same are skipped. The three rows above become this one line:

 

{
  "DocDate": "2026-10-25",
  "StockTransferLines": [{
    "ItemCode": "ITEM2001", "Quantity": 6,
    "FromWarehouseCode": "01", "WarehouseCode": "W812",
    "BatchNumbers": [
      {"BatchNumber": "BT1", "Quantity": 1},
      {"BatchNumber": "BT2", "Quantity": 2},
      {"BatchNumber": "BT3", "Quantity": 3}
    ]
  }]
}

The batch quantities have to add up to the line quantity, and if the item belongs to a UoM group the line also needs a UoMEntry.

 

Posting and validation

After logging in through /b1s/v1/Login, the document is sent as a JSON POST to /b1s/v1/StockTransfers, or to /b1s/v1/StockTransferDrafts when it should be checked in SAP first. SAP validates it like any other entry and nothing touches the database directly. If SAP rejects the document, the error comes back as it is, so the row can be fixed and the run repeated.

Instead of a script, I built a small Windows app for this, called Batch Transfer. It runs separately from SAP and talks to it only through the Service Layer.

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

A draft run on demo data: ITEM2001 moving from warehouse 01 to W812 with three batches.

Conclusion

Selecting batches line by line is slow when an item has many of them. With one Excel sheet, the whole transfer goes to SAP as a single Stock Transfer, validated like any other document. If a row is rejected, the error points to it, so you fix that row and run again.

Prepared by

Amirhossein Tonekaboni
SAP Business One Consultant

entry.title: Transition to SuccessFactors from non SAP system in an M&A engagement
entry.content:
Transition to SuccessFactors from non SAP system in an M&A engagement

Lift and shift or harmonize? A high-level guide to the critical focus areas

 

Applies when the parent runs on SAP SuccessFactors and acquired company runs on a different HR platform like Workday.

Summary

When an acquired company runs on a non-SAP HCM platform and the parent runs on SAP SuccessFactors, the integration is rarely a single decision. It is a series of area-by-area choices between two paths: lift and shift the acquired company's way of working or harmonize onto the parent's standards.

Two ways to bring an acquired population into the parent system

LIFT AND SHIFT

HARMONIZE

•     Keep the acquired structures

•     Fastest path and lowest Day 1 risk (based upon TSA timeline)

•     Honors commitments to employees

•     Creates clean-up work after go-live

•     Adopt the parent's standards

•     Unified structure, cleaner analytics

•     Needs HR and business alignment

•     Higher change impact for employees on day 1

 

Part A: Foundation Areas

These areas define how people, jobs, and organizations are represented in SuccessFactors Employee Central.

1. Job Architecture

Job codes, job families, levels and grades, job profiles, titles

Lift and shift

Carry the acquired company's job codes and titles into SuccessFactors as-is, utilizing existing job families and adding new.

Harmonize

Map all acquired roles into the parent's existing job architecture before load.

Focus areas

•     Mapping Workday job profiles to EC job classifications

•     Preserving FLSA/exempt status and EEO and other compliance fields

•     Level calibration, pay range impact, and title changes if harmonizing

•     Impact on compa-ratio for compensation module

Best practice

Lift and shift for Day 1 so harmonization can happen later without rework, unless the role mapping is obvious and already approved.

 

2. Organization Structure and Legal Entities

Supervisory orgs vs. departments, cost centers, legal entities, positions

Lift and shift

Recreate the acquired structure as a standalone branch in the parent's org tree.

Harmonize

Fold teams into the parent's departments, cost centers, and reporting lines.

Focus areas

•     Legal entity and cost center setup (finance and payroll dependencies)

•     Position management vs. non-position models

•     Manager hierarchy accuracy and approval chains (OrgLab can be used to define future state reporting structure)

•     Employees with dotted-line or matrix relationships

Best practice

Keep a clear structure as much as possible at go-live, then you can align in planned waves based upon finance and legal entity decisions.

 

3. Compensation and Benefits Structures

Pay grades, salary ranges, bonus plans, benefit plans, merit cycles

Lift and shift

Preserve existing pay structures and plan eligibility to honor commitments.

Harmonize

Move employees to the parent's structures and programs.

Focus areas

•     There may be Legal or contractual obligations to maintain pay and benefits for a defined period

•     Country-specific compensation plans

•     Integration with payroll and benefits vendors

•     Alignment of merit and bonus cycles with the go-live

Best practice

Cover the existing terms at transition. Harmonization can be done later with job architecture harmonization

 

4. Business Rules and Workflows

Approvals, hire/term/transfer rules,event reasons

Lift and shift

Replicate acquired company processes in SuccessFactors as closely as possible.

Harmonize

Adopt the parent's standard workflows and rules.

Focus areas

•     Workday business processes do not map one-to-one to SF workflows and business rules

•     Defaults such as work schedule hours at hire

•     Termination logic and workflow conditions

•     Event and reason code alignment

Best practice

Default to the parent's standard processes. Replicating acquired company logic in SF usually adds complexity at go-live. Make exceptions only for legal or country needs for a successful go-live

 

5. Security and Access (RBP)

Role-based permissions, groups, sensitive data, single sign-on

Lift and shift

Replicate the acquired company's security roles.

Harmonize

Build access on the parent's role and group model.

Focus areas

•     Rebuild in RBP groups and roles rather than copying Workday/third party security to avoid continuing security policies that were not effective

•     Target population groups for the acquired company

•     Country-based restrictions

•     Tighter controls sensitive data such as dependents, national IDs

Best practice

Always harmonize. Replicating another platform's security model is not recommended

 

6. Country Configuration and Compliance

New countries, statutory fields, data privacy, regulatory reporting

Lift and shift

Configure acquired countries as stand-alone setups with their own picklists, fields, and templates.

Harmonize

Align to the parent's country configurations where they already exist.

Focus areas

•     Statutory fields and local labor law requirements

•     New country setup where the parent has no footprint

•     Document and contract templates by country

•     Regulatory reporting continuity (for example EEO and VETS-4212 in the US)

•     Data privacy requirements such as GDPR

Best practice

Build a country-by-country readiness checklist with local HR and Legal sign-off. Reuse the parent's configuration where it exists and add only the gaps.

 

7. Historical Data

Effective-dated history, archives, retention, right of access

Lift and shift

Load as much history as the data model allows.

Harmonize

Load current state record into SuccessFactors

Focus areas

•     Full history should not be converted

•     Retention policy and who can access the archive after transition

•     GDPR right of access

•     Former employees' future needs: tax, immigration, benefits, legal matters

Best practice

This is often underestimated and surfaces late, usually when a former employee or auditor asks for records that no longer exist in the new system. Define the retention and access model early: where history lives, who can access it, and how former employees can request their records.

 

Part B: Talent Modules

8. Performance and Goals Management (PMGM)

Goals, review cycles, ratings, calibration, feedback, development plans

Performance touches pay, promotion, and how employees feel about being evaluated by a new company. It is also closely scrutinized by works councils.

 

Lift and shift

Build separate templates, rating scales, and cycle dates in SF for the acquired population.

Harmonize

Assign acquired employees to the parent's existing forms, scale, and calendar.

Focus areas

•     Template and permission assignment by population

•     Rating scale crosswalk (for example 5-point to 4-point or 5-point to 5-point) – determine how past ratings map

•     Route maps and calibration sessions that include the new group

•     RBP visibility for ratings and feedback

•     Performance history of employees

•     Complete in flight cycle in legacy system

Best Practice

Honor the in-flight cycle through completion, then onboard the acquired population into the parent's process at the start of the next cycle. Build a rating scale crosswalk and archive historical ratings with controlled access. In Scenario B, skip building a temporary SF process if the parent will not use that module.

 

 

9. Recruitment and Talent Acquisition

Requisitions, candidates, offers, onboarding handoff, compliance reporting

Hiring does not pause on go-live day. Open requisitions, in-flight candidates, and offers must continue, and offers are legally sensitive.

 

Lift and shift

Create separate requisition templates, approval flows, and offer letter templates for the acquired population.

Harmonize

Use the parent's templates, workflows, and career site.

Focus areas

•     Requisition and offer approval workflows

•     Requisition templates tied to job architecture

•     Onboarding handoff to EC and country-specific fields

Best Practice

Harmonize while protecting in-flight offers.

10. Learning

Catalog, curricula, assignments, transcripts, compliance training

Lift and shift

Migrate the acquired company's courses, curricula, and assignments.

Harmonize

Move the acquired population into the parent's catalog and assignment model.

Focus areas

•     Completion records and certifications that are compliance-critical

•     Assignment profiles and exclusion rules, so parent-company mandatory assignments do not flood the acquired population unintentionally

•     Content licensing

•     Access for employees and managers

Best practice

Migrate completion records for compliance-critical items only. Use exclusion rules to control assignments, then phase the acquired population into the parent catalog on a planned schedule.

 

Part C: Operations and Experience

These areas keep people paid, informed, and productive from the first day on the new platform.

11. Time Off and Work Schedules

Leave policies, accruals, balances, holiday calendars, default hours

Lift and shift

Recreate the acquired policies and accrual rules, and carry over balances.

Harmonize

Move to the parent's policies.

Focus areas

•     Policy gaps in countries where the parent has no equivalent (manual tracking or a vendor solution)

•     Work schedule defaults, such as hours defaulting at new hire

•     Configure work schedules for time off calculations

•     Holiday calendars by location

Best practice

Lift and shift at go-live. Changing leave policies mid-transition can create issues. Flag country gaps early and decide on manual or vendor tracking.

 

12. Employee Experience and Language Support

Self-service, mobile, documents, language, help desk, communications

Lift and shift

Provide a separate portal or landing experience for the acquired population.

Harmonize

Move employees to the parent's portal, mobile app, and support model.

Focus areas

•     Employee and manager self-service readiness

•     Language support gaps in the UI and translated job aids

•     Help desk and case routing for the new population

•     Communications and training before and after cutover

Best practice

Use the parent's company experience, and close language gaps before go-live. Translated materials also support the works council conversation.

entry.title: SAP FI Posting Really Works From FB50 to BKPF, BSEG, and ACDOCA
entry.content:
For many SAP Finance consultants, posting a journal entry is one of the first activities we learn. Open FB50, enter the accounts and amounts, make sure debit equals credit, and post.

The result looks simple: debit one account and credit another. But what actually happens inside SAP when we click Post? Where does the document go? What is stored in BKPF? What is stored in BSEG? Why do we also have ACDOCA in SAP S/4HANA? And when troubleshooting a posting, which object should a functional consultant investigate?

In this walkthrough, we will follow one simple G/L posting from FB50 to the posted accounting document and then into the underlying accounting data. The objective is not just to post a journal entry, but to understand how the user-facing transaction relates to SAP's accounting structures.

Assume we need to record an office expense of USD 1,000. The simplified accounting entry is:

Line

Account

Debit

Credit

1

Reserve Defer'd Tax

$1,00

 

2

Payroll Bonus

 

$1,00

For this exercise, we use transaction FB50 - Enter G/L Account Document. The exact company code, G/L accounts, cost center, and other organizational values will depend on your sandbox.

Figure 1: Sample G/L journal entry entered using FB50

Figure 1 establishes the transaction used throughout this article. The header represents information that applies to the overall accounting document, while the lower section contains the accounting line items.

FB50 provides a single-screen way to enter a G/L account document. From the user's perspective, the transaction combines document-level information with line-item information.

Header information

  1. Company Code
  2. Document Date
  3. Posting Date
  4. Document Type
  5. Currency
  6. Reference
  7. Header Text

Line-item information

  1. G/L Account
  2. Debit or Credit Amount
  3. Tax Code
  4. Cost Center
  5. Profit Center
  6. Assignment
  7. Item Text

Other account assignments depending on configuration

This distinction becomes important later because the accounting document is not represented by one single table containing every field in exactly the same way.

Before Posting: SAP Validates the Document

Clicking Post does not mean SAP simply writes the screen values directly to the database. The document must first satisfy the posting controls and checks that apply to the transaction and configuration.

At a high level, think of the process as:

User Input → Validation → Derivation → Accounting Document Creation → Database Update

Depending on the scenario, SAP may evaluate items such as:

  1. Is the company code valid?
  2. Is the posting period open?
  3. Is the G/L account valid and open for posting?
  4. Are mandatory fields populated according to field status?
  5. Are account assignments such as cost center valid on the posting date?
  6. Do debits and credits balance?
  7. Are document-type and posting-key rules satisfied?
  8. Do validations, substitutions, or enhancements apply?

In our simple example, the document must balance: debit USD 1,000 and credit USD 1,000, producing a zero document balance.

Simulate Before Posting

Before posting, use the simulation functionality where appropriate. Simulation is useful because it allows you to review the accounting result before the document is committed.

Do not assume that the number of lines entered by the user will always equal the final accounting representation. More complex scenarios can introduce taxes, automatically generated lines, account determination, document splitting, or other ledger-relevant information.

 As shown in Figure 2, the simulation gives us a checkpoint: this is the accounting result we expect SAP to create when we post.

Post the Document

Once the document passes the relevant checks, click Post. SAP generates an accounting document number according to the configured number range.

Record the Company Code, Accounting Document Number, and Fiscal Year. These values become the key for the rest of the investigation.

 

 

Display the Posted Document in FB03

Before going to the database tables, first review the document from the functional user's perspective. Open FB03 and display the document that was just posted.

Figure 4 represents the posted document as a functional consultant would normally review it. We will now use the same document key to inspect the underlying accounting data.

 

First Stop: BKPF - Accounting Document Header

Open SE16N and enter table BKPF. Filter using the same Company Code, Accounting Document, and Fiscal Year.

Recommended selection:

BUKRS = <your company code>
BELNR = <your posted document number>
GJAHR = <fiscal year>

BKPF represents accounting document header information. Conceptually, it answers questions about the document as a whole.

From Figure 5, we can quickly identify the document type, dates, fiscal period, currency, originating transaction, and user-related header information. For many support investigations, BKPF is an efficient first checkpoint.

Second Stop: BSEG - Operational Accounting Items

Next, open SE16N for BSEG and use the same document key. Instead of one header record, you will see the operational accounting document items.

The operational accounting items shown in Figure 6 should be compared with the lines previously displayed in FB03. This is the bridge between the user-facing accounting document and the technical representation of its entry items.

Enter ACDOCA - The Universal Journal

In SAP S/4HANA, the investigation should not stop at BSEG. Open SE16N for ACDOCA and filter the same accounting document.

ACDOCA is the Universal Journal line-item table. It brings together a broad set of accounting and reporting dimensions that are central to S/4HANA Finance.

Depending on your scenario and configuration, useful fields can include:

  1. RLDNR - Ledger
  2. RBUKRS - Company Code
  3. GJAHR - Fiscal Year
  4. BELNR - Accounting Document
  5. DOCLN - Universal Journal line item
  6. RACCT - G/L Account
  7. RCNTR - Cost Center
  8. PRCTR - Profit Center
  9. SEGMENT - Segment
  10. Relevant currency and amount fields for your posting

Is BSEG Replaced by ACDOCA?

A common simplification is: "In S/4HANA, ACDOCA replaced BSEG." That statement is too broad.

BSEG still exists and remains important for operational accounting-document information. ACDOCA represents the Universal Journal. A more useful troubleshooting model is:

BKPF → Document header
BSEG → Operational / entry-view accounting information
ACDOCA → Universal Journal and ledger-oriented accounting information

The correct object depends on the question you are trying to answer. Functional troubleshooting becomes faster when you first decide whether you are investigating the document header, operational line-item behavior, or the Universal Journal representation.

Entry View vs. General Ledger View

For a basic two-line posting, the entry view and the General Ledger representation may look very similar. However, more complex scenarios can introduce additional ledger-relevant information or generated lines.

Document splitting is a good example. A transaction entered with only a few business lines can result in additional lines in the General Ledger view so that required reporting dimensions remain balanced.

Which Universal Journal dimensions were generated?

ACDOCA

The important lesson is not to troubleshoot an S/4HANA accounting document by looking at only one table. Start with the business question, and then select the object that represents that layer of the transaction.

Simplified Conceptual Flow

The following diagram should be created as a simple PowerPoint or diagram image and inserted into the blog. Label it as a simplified conceptual view so readers do not interpret it as the exact ABAP execution or physical database-write sequence.

Why This Matters During Production Support

Consider a support ticket: "The profit center is incorrect on accounting document 1900000123."

A stronger troubleshooting path is:

  1. Identify the document and header context in BKPF.
  2. Understand the operational accounting items in BSEG.
  3. Examine the Universal Journal representation in ACDOCA.
  4. Determine where the expected and actual values first diverge.

Functional Consultants Should Understand the Technical Layer

A functional consultant does not need to become an ABAP developer to benefit from understanding SAP's technical architecture. Knowing how to move from transaction to accounting document to database structures can dramatically improve troubleshooting.

Instead of asking only, "Why did SAP not populate the profit center?" a more precise investigation is: "Was the profit center present in the operational entry view, and what value ultimately reached the Universal Journal?"

Trace the responsible derivation, configuration, substitution, enhancement, or integration logic.

This approach can help with issues involving cost centers, profit centers, segments, currencies, clearing, document splitting, account determination, interfaces, substitutions, and enhancements.

Key Takeaways

  1. FB50 is only the starting point; SAP performs validation and derivation before a document is persisted.
  2. BKPF is the primary place to understand accounting document header information.
  3. BSEG remains relevant for operational accounting-document line items in S/4HANA.
  4. ACDOCA contains the Universal Journal line-item representation and ledger/reporting dimensions.
  5. The same accounting document should be traced across FB03, BKPF, BSEG, and ACDOCA to understand the complete picture.
  6. For support issues, identify the layer where the value first differs before jumping directly to configuration or code.

entry.title: M&A Engagements: Works Council Engagement - A Gating Item for HR System Migrations
entry.content:
HR TECHNOLOGY M&A INTEGRATION

Works Council Engagement: A Gating Item for HR

System Migrations

Co-determination, consultation, and approval rights over HR systems and employee data

 

Who this is for: program leads, HRIS teams, Legal, and Privacy teams moving an acquired workforce onto a new HR platform (for example from Workday into SAP SuccessFactors) where acquired employees sit in countries with works councils.

1. Why this is a gating item

Works council engagement is not a lift and shift vs. harmonize choice. In countries with works councils, the council often has legal rights to be informed, consulted, or to approve a new HR system before employee data can move. Missing this can delay go-live regardless of how ready the technology is.

The core message

A system can be fully configured, tested, and signed off by the business, and still be blocked at the last step. Treat works council approval as a formal go-live readiness criterion, owned and tracked like any other critical-path item.

 

What is at stake if it is skipped

Country example

Possible consequence of proceeding without the required process

Germany

The council can seek injunctive relief to stop use of a monitoring-capable system until co-determination is respected, and the matter can end up before a conciliation committee.

Netherlands

A decision taken without required consent can be declared void if the council invokes this in time, and the council can contest the decision.

France

Courts have ordered deployments of new tools suspended until the information and consultation procedure is completed, in some cases with daily penalties.

All countries

Delayed go-live, loss of trust with the workforce, rework of design decisions, and reputational and legal exposure.

 

2. Understand the rights you are dealing with

Not every council right is the same. The strength of the right changes what you must prepare and how long the process can take. In practice, three levels matter.

The spectrum of works council rights

INFORM

→

CONSULT

→

CONSENT

Council receives the facts

before decisions are final

 

Council gives an opinion

and the employer must hear it

before deciding

 

No lawful rollout without

agreement, or a substitute

ruling or conciliation

Typical for: early information on planned technical systems (for example Germany, Sec. 90 BetrVG)

 

Typical for: France, where the CSE is informed and consulted on new technology and on tools that monitor activity

 

Typical for: Germany (Sec. 87 BetrVG) and the Netherlands (Art. 27 WOR) for systems that can monitor or that process personnel data

Rights differ by country and by what the system does. Always confirm with local counsel.

 

Why HR systems usually trigger these rights

  • An HR platform holds personnel data, and rules about processing and protecting that data are often subject to council rights.
  • Several statutes look at capability, not intent. A system that can observe or record behavior or performance can trigger consent rights even if the employer promises not to use it that way.
  • Talent modules go further. Performance, goals, and assessment criteria are frequently treated as evaluation schemes, which have their own consent or consultation rules.
  • Analytics, dashboards, and AI-assisted features can widen the scope. Switching a feature on later can reopen the discussion.

 

How the level shapes your plan

Level

What it means for the program

Plan for

Inform

No veto, but early notice builds trust and avoids disputes later

•     Brief the council early

•     Share a dossier summary and a named contact

Consult

The council's opinion must be heard before the decision is taken, so timing matters

•     Allow a real review period

•     Document how feedback was handled

•     Decide only after consultation closes

Consent

The council can withhold agreement, which may lead to negotiation, conciliation, or a court route

•     Treat as critical path

•     Negotiate a written agreement

•     Prepare a contingency per country

 

3. What works councils typically focus on

Councils generally ask the same core questions, even when the legal basis differs. Preparing a clear answer to each, in writing and in the local language, is the single most effective way to shorten the process.

Topic

What the council asks

What to bring

Data

What employee data is collected, what moves to the new system, and why it is needed

•     Field-level data inventory: field, source, target, purpose

•     Rationale for each category, and what is not migrated

Data security

Where data is hosted, how it is protected, and who else can touch it

•     Hosting location, encryption, cross-border transfer mechanism

•     Vendor and sub-processor list with access scope

Data access

Who can see what, and how sensitive fields are protected

•     Role and permission matrix (managers, HR, support, offshore teams)

•     Live demo of what each role sees, including sensitive fields

Historical data

What is retained, what is archived, and how people can reach their records

•     Retention schedule and archive location

•     Process for current and former employees to request records

Monitoring

Assurance that the system will not be used to watch individuals

•     Written statement of purposes and prohibited uses

•     Status of analytics and AI features (on, off, planned)

Language

Whether employees can understand and use the system

•     Translated job aids, notices, and training

•     Known language gaps and the mitigation

Employee rights

How access, correction, and deletion requests are handled

•     GDPR rights process and contacts

•     Employee notice and communication plan

 

Tip: share the data model, not the data

The inventory should describe data elements and purposes, not individual employee records. Disclosing personal data to the council can itself need a legal basis, so keep examples anonymized or in test data.

 

4. A practical engagement approach

Run the works council track as its own workstream with an owner, a plan, and a status line in the program dashboard. A five-phase approach keeps Legal, Privacy, HR, and the program team aligned.

Five phases of works council engagement

1  Scope

2  Prepare

3  Brief and demo

4  Agree

5  Sustain

•     Identify entities and countries

•     Confirm council exists and level (local or central)

•     Agree owners and timeline

•     Align Legal, Privacy, HR on one answer set

•     Translate key materials

•     Early briefing, before design is final

•     Live demos of security and access

•     Log questions and commitments

•     Negotiate works agreement or opinion

•     Resolve open points in writing

•     Obtain formal approval or consultation close

•     Track as go-live criterion

•     Re-open if scope changes

•     Keep a named contact post go-live

 

Best practices

  • Engage early, before design is final. Councils want to shape decisions, not rubber-stamp them.
  • Bring a field-level data inventory showing what is migrated and why.
  • Run live demos of the actual security model, role access, and what managers can see.
  • Give one set of answers. Align Legal, Privacy, and local HR, and document commitments in a works agreement where required.
  • Plan for their cycle. Build review cycles (weeks to months) into the plan, provide translated materials and a named contact, and track approval as a formal go-live readiness criterion.

entry.title: My First SAP RAP Application – Part 2: Advanced RAP Features with Managed RAP
entry.content:
Hello SAP Community! 👋

Welcome to Part 2 of my SAP RAP learning journey!

In my previous blog, "My First SAP RAP Application: Building a Student Management App Using Managed RAP," I explained how I created a simple Student Management Application from scratch using the SAP ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP).

The application supported basic CRUD operations using Managed RAP and SAP Fiori Elements.

https://community.sap.com/t5/abap-blog-posts/my-first-sap-rap-application-building-a-student-management-app-using/ba-p/14506725 

In this second part, I will share how I enhanced the same application by adding more advanced RAP features.

The goal was to move beyond basic CRUD and understand how to implement real business logic and improve the user experience.

What Are We Going to Build?

We will enhance our existing Student Management Application with five features:

  1. Selection Fields — Filter students directly from the Fiori List Report.

  2. Validations — Prevent saving students with invalid ages.

  3. Determinations — Automatically set the initial student status.

  4. Custom Actions — Approve selected students using a custom button.

  5. Draft Handling — Save unfinished changes and continue editing later.

Development Environment

  • SAP S/4HANA 2023 FPS01

  • ABAP Development Tools (ADT) in Eclipse

  • ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model

  • Managed Business Object

  • SAP Fiori Elements

  • OData V2 UI for the original application

  • OData V4 UI for the draft-enabled application

We will reuse the following objects from Part 1:

Object Name

Database TableZSTD_TABLE_DEMO
Interface CDS ViewZ_I_STD
Projection CDS ViewZ_C_STD
Base Behavior DefinitionZ_I_STD
Behavior PoolZBP_I_STD
Projection Behavior DefinitionZ_C_STD
Service DefinitionZ_SD_STD

Let's get started!

My Personal Experience

After successfully building my first Student Management Application using Managed RAP, I wanted to take the next step and explore more advanced RAP features through hands-on practice.

I started by adding Selection Fields to improve filtering in the Fiori List Report. Then, I implemented a Validation for student age and a Determination to automatically assign the status NEW when creating a student.

One of my favorite parts was implementing the Approve Student action. It was interesting to see how a custom action defined in the RAP Behavior Definition could be implemented in the Behavior Pool and exposed as a button in SAP Fiori Elements.

The most challenging part for me was Draft Handling. I initially faced an error related to draft persistence. After configuring and generating the Draft Table correctly, I was able to create a student, leave the page without activating the record, and find the unfinished record again using the Own Draft filter.

This experience helped me better understand how RAP handles business logic, transactional processing, and draft management.

AI Disclosure: I used ChatGPT to help organize, structure, and improve the English writing of this article. The development, troubleshooting, and testing described in this blog are based on my hands-on SAP RAP learning experience.

1. Adding Selection Fields to the Fiori List Report

The first enhancement was adding filters to the application.

Previously, our List Report displayed student records, but we wanted users to filter the results by Student Name and Student Class.

SAP Fiori Elements allows us to configure these filters using UI annotations.

Step 1: Open the Metadata Extension

Open the Metadata Extension of Z_C_STD.

Add the @UI.selectionField annotation to the relevant fields.

@UI.lineItem: [{ position: 20, label: 'Student Name' }]
@UI.identification: [{ position: 20, label: 'Student Name' }]
@UI.selectionField: [{ position: 10 }]
Studentname;

@UI.lineItem: [{ position: 30, label: 'Student Class' }]
@UI.identification: [{ position: 30, label: 'Student Class' }]
@UI.selectionField: [{ position: 20 }]
Studentclass;

Explanation

The annotation @UI.selectionField tells Fiori Elements to display the specified field in the Filter Bar.

The position property determines the order of the filters.

The important point is that we did not need to write any custom SAPUI5 or JavaScript code.

After activating the Metadata Extension and refreshing the Fiori application, the new filters appeared automatically.

Key Learning

@UI.selectionField Provides field-specific filtering. It is different from the global free-text search feature, which uses @searchannotations.

2. Implementing a Validation for Student Age

Next, I wanted to implement a simple business rule.

Our requirement was:

A student's age must be between 5 and 100.

If the user enters an age outside this range, the application must prevent the final save and display an error message.

Step 1: Define the Validation in the Base Behavior Definition

Open the Base Behavior Definition of Z_I_STD.

Add the following code inside the behavior entity:

validation ValidateStudentAge on save
{
  create;
  field Studentage;
}

Explanation

  • validation defines a business rule.

  • ValidateStudentAge is the name of our validation.

  • on save means the validation runs during the save sequence.

  • create triggers the validation when creating a student.

  • field Studentage triggers it when the age field is changed.

Step 2: Implement the Validation in the Behavior Pool

Open the Behavior Pool ZBP_I_STD.

In the local handler class, declare the method:

METHODS validateStudentAge FOR VALIDATE ON SAVE
  IMPORTING keys FOR _studentdetail~ValidateStudentAge.

Then implement the method:

METHOD validateStudentAge.

  READ ENTITIES OF Z_I_STD IN LOCAL MODE
    ENTITY _studentdetail
    FIELDS ( Studentage )
    WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
    RESULT DATA(lt_students).

  LOOP AT lt_students INTO DATA(ls_student).

    DATA(lv_age) = CONV i( ls_student-Studentage ).

    IF lv_age < 5 OR lv_age > 100.

      APPEND VALUE #(
        %tky = ls_student-%tky
      ) TO failed-_studentdetail.

      APPEND VALUE #(
        %tky = ls_student-%tky
        %msg = new_message_with_text(
          severity = if_abap_behv_message=>severity-error
          text     = 'Student age must be between 5 and 100'
        )
        %element-Studentage = if_abap_behv=>mk-on
      ) TO reported-_studentdetail.

    ENDIF.

  ENDLOOP.

ENDMETHOD.

How Does It Work?

The implementation has three main parts.

READ ENTITIES

Reads student data from the RAP transactional buffer, including changes that have not yet been persisted to the database.

FAILED

Identifies the student instances whose save operation must be rejected.

REPORTED

Returns an error message to the consumer and identifies the field containing the invalid value.

Step 3: Test the Validation

Open the Fiori application and try creating a student with:

  • Student Age = 120 → Save should fail.

  • Student Age = 25 → Save should succeed.

Key Learning

RAP Validations allow us to enforce business rules in the backend.

This is important because the validation is not limited to a particular UI.

For more advanced draft scenarios, state messages and message lifecycle handling should also be considered.

3. Using Determinations to Set the Initial Student Status

After implementing the validation, I wanted to automate a small business process.

The requirement was:

Whenever a new student is created, the application should automatically set the student status to NEW.

This is a perfect use case for a RAP Determination.

Step 1: Add a Status Field to the Database Table

Open ZSTD_TABLE_DEMO and add:

student_status : abap.char(10);

This field stores the student status.

We will use two values:

  • NEW

  • APPROVED

Step 2: Extend the Interface CDS View

In Z_I_STD, add:

student_status as StudentStatus

Step 3: Extend the Projection CDS View

In Z_C_STD, expose the new field:

StudentStatus

Step 4: Display the Status in Fiori

In the Metadata Extension, add:

@UI.lineItem: [{ position: 60, label: 'Student Status' }]
@UI.identification: [{ position: 60, label: 'Student Status' }]
StudentStatus;

Step 5: Define the Determination

In the Base Behavior Definition, add:

field ( readonly ) StudentStatus;

determination SetInitialStatus on modify
{
  create;
}

Explanation

on modify tells RAP to execute the determination during the modify phase when its trigger condition is met.

The create trigger means it runs when a new student instance is created.

We marked StudentStatus as read-only so the consumer cannot freely change it. Our backend logic will manage its value.

Step 6: Implement the Determination

In the Behavior Pool, declare:

METHODS SetInitialStatus FOR DETERMINE ON MODIFY
  IMPORTING keys FOR _studentdetail~SetInitialStatus.

Implementation:

METHOD SetInitialStatus.

  READ ENTITIES OF Z_I_STD IN LOCAL MODE
    ENTITY _studentdetail
    FIELDS ( StudentStatus )
    WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
    RESULT DATA(lt_students).

  DELETE lt_students WHERE StudentStatus IS NOT INITIAL.

  CHECK lt_students IS NOT INITIAL.

  MODIFY ENTITIES OF Z_I_STD IN LOCAL MODE
    ENTITY _studentdetail
    UPDATE FIELDS ( StudentStatus )
    WITH VALUE #(
      FOR ls_student IN lt_students
      (
        %tky          = ls_student-%tky
        StudentStatus = 'NEW'
      )
    ).

ENDMETHOD.

How Does It Work?

First, we read the Student Status.

If the status is already filled, we do not overwrite it.

If the status is empty, we update it to NEW using MODIFY ENTITIES IN LOCAL MODE.

Since this is Managed RAP, the framework handles persistence when the active instance is saved.

Step 7: Test the Determination

Create a student in Fiori.

The Student Status should be set automatically to NEW.

Key Learning

A Validation checks whether data is valid.

A Determination automatically calculates or changes data when defined trigger conditions are met.

4. Creating a Custom Action: Approve Student

Now that every new student receives the status NEW, I wanted to add a button that allows the user to approve a selected student.

The business requirement was:

Select a student in the List Report, click Approve Student, and change the status from NEW to APPROVED.

In RAP, we can achieve this using a Custom Instance Action.

Step 1: Define the Action in the Base Behavior Definition

Open the Base BDEF Z_I_STD and add:

action ( authorization : update ) ApproveStudent
  result [1] $self;

Explanation

  • action defines a custom business operation.

  • ApproveStudent is the action name.

  • authorization : update reuses update authorization for this action.

  • result [1] $self returns the updated student instance.

Step 2: Expose the Action in the Projection Behavior Definition

Open the Projection BDEF Z_C_STD and add:

use action ApproveStudent;

The Base Behavior Definition defines the action, while the Projection Behavior Definition makes it available to the service consumer.

Step 3: Implement the Action in the Behavior Pool

Declare the method:

METHODS ApproveStudent FOR MODIFY
  IMPORTING keys FOR ACTION _studentdetail~ApproveStudent
  RESULT result.

Implementation:

METHOD ApproveStudent.

  MODIFY ENTITIES OF Z_I_STD IN LOCAL MODE
    ENTITY _studentdetail
    UPDATE FIELDS ( StudentStatus )
    WITH VALUE #(
      FOR key IN keys
      (
        %tky          = key-%tky
        StudentStatus = 'APPROVED'
      )
    ).

  READ ENTITIES OF Z_I_STD IN LOCAL MODE
    ENTITY _studentdetail
    ALL FIELDS
    WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
    RESULT DATA(lt_students).

  result = VALUE #(
    FOR ls_student IN lt_students
    (
      %tky   = ls_student-%tky
      %param = ls_student
    )
  ).

ENDMETHOD.

Explanation

The method receives the keys of the selected students.

Using MODIFY ENTITIES, it changes their status to APPROVED.

Then it reads the updated instances and returns them to the consumer.

Step 4: Add the Action Button to the Fiori List Report

To display the action in the application, update the StudentStatus annotations in the Metadata Extension.

@UI.lineItem: [
  { position: 60, label: 'Student Status' },
  {
    type: #FOR_ACTION,
    dataAction: 'ApproveStudent',
    label: 'Approve Student'
  }
]
@UI.identification: [{ position: 60, label: 'Student Status' }]
StudentStatus;

The #FOR_ACTION annotation allows Fiori Elements to generate the action button automatically.

Step 5: Test the Action

Open the List Report, select a student whose status is NEW, and click Approve Student.

The status should change to APPROVED.

Key Learning

RAP Actions allow us to implement custom business operations beyond standard CRUD.

In a future enhancement, Dynamic Feature Control could be used to disable the Approve action for students who are already approved.

5. Enabling Draft Handling

The final enhancement was Draft Handling.

This feature was particularly interesting because it allows users to work on unfinished data without immediately activating it as a final database record.

For example, a user might start entering student information, leave the application, and return later to continue editing.

What Is Draft Handling?

Draft Handling separates unfinished changes from active business data.

A draft-enabled RAP Business Object supports operations such as:

  • Edit

  • Resume

  • Activate

  • Discard

  • Prepare

The RAP framework manages the draft lifecycle.

Step 1: Add Timestamp Fields to the Database Table

Open ZSTD_TABLE_DEMO and add:

last_changed_at       : abp_lastchange_tstmpl;
local_last_changed_at : abp_locinst_lastchange_tstmpl;

These fields are used to track changes and support ETag-based concurrency control.

Step 2: Extend the Interface CDS View

Add the following fields to Z_I_STD:

@Semantics.systemDateTime.lastChangedAt: true
last_changed_at as LastChangedAt,

@Semantics.systemDateTime.localInstanceLastChangedAt: true
local_last_changed_at as LocalLastChangedAt

The semantic annotations allow the managed runtime to maintain the corresponding administrative timestamps.

Step 3: Extend the Projection CDS View

Expose the following field in Z_C_STD:

LocalLastChangedAt

LastChangedAt is used as the total ETag for draft processing and does not need to be exposed through this projection.

Step 4: Enable Draft in the Base Behavior Definition

Add with draft; and configure the draft persistence and ETags.

The following example shows the final Base Behavior Definition after including the enhancements from this blog:

managed implementation in class zbp_i_std unique;
strict ( 2 );

with draft;

define behavior for Z_I_STD alias _studentdetail
persistent table zstd_table_demo
draft table zstd_table_d
lock master
total etag LastChangedAt
authorization master ( instance )
etag master LocalLastChangedAt
{
  create;
  update;
  delete;

  field ( readonly, numbering : managed ) Rollno;
  field ( readonly ) StudentStatus;
  field ( readonly ) LastChangedAt, LocalLastChangedAt;

  validation ValidateStudentAge on save
  {
    create;
    field Studentage;
  }

  determination SetInitialStatus on modify
  {
    create;
  }

  action ( authorization : update ) ApproveStudent
    result [1] $self;

  draft action Edit;
  draft action Activate;
  draft action Discard;
  draft action Resume;

  draft determine action Prepare
  {
    validation ValidateStudentAge;
  }

  mapping for zstd_table_demo
  {
    Rollno             = rollno;
    Studentname        = studentname;
    Studentclass       = studentclass;
    Studentage         = studentage;
    Schoolname         = schoolname;
    StudentStatus      = student_status;
    LastChangedAt      = last_changed_at;
    LocalLastChangedAt = local_last_changed_at;
  }
}

Explanation

with draft

Enables Draft Handling for the Business Object.

draft table

Specifies the database table that stores draft instances.

total etag

Supports consistency checks between active and draft data.

etag master

Supports optimistic concurrency control.

draft actions

Provide the standard draft lifecycle operations.

Prepare

Allows the age validation to be executed as part of preparing a draft for activation.

Step 5: Generate the Draft Table

In Eclipse ADT:

  1. Place the cursor on zstd_table_d in the Behavior Definition.

  2. Press Ctrl + 1.

  3. Choose the available Quick Fix to generate the Draft Table.

  4. Complete the wizard.

  5. Activate the generated table and the Behavior Definition.

The draft persistence table contains the business fields and the required draft administration structure.

Step 6: Update the Projection Behavior Definition

Open the Projection BDEF Z_C_STD.

The final version looks like this:

projection;
strict ( 2 );

use draft;

define behavior for Z_C_STD alias _studentdetail
use etag
{
  use create;
  use update;
  use delete;

  use action ApproveStudent;

  use action Edit;
  use action Activate;
  use action Discard;
  use action Resume;
  use action Prepare;
}

Explanation

The statement use draft; exposes Draft Handling through the projection.

The draft actions make the lifecycle operations available to the consumer.

Step 7: Create an OData V4 UI Service Binding

For the draft-enabled application, I created a new Service Binding.

Service Binding: Z_UI_STD_O4

Binding Type: OData V4 - UI

I reused the existing Service Definition:

define service Z_SD_STD {
  expose Z_C_STD;
}

After activating and publishing the new Service Binding, I launched the Fiori Elements preview.

Step 8: Test Draft Handling in Fiori

The first test was straightforward.

I started creating a new student and entered some information without completing the final save.

Then I left the editing page.

When I returned to the List Report, the draft was still available.

This confirmed that my unfinished data could be retained and accessed again.

To test the remaining draft lifecycle, we can:

  1. Open the draft and resume editing.

  2. Save to activate the student.

  3. Verify that the active student record is persisted.

  4. Create another draft and discard it.

  5. Confirm that the discarded record is not activated.

Editing Status Filter

After enabling Draft Handling, I also noticed a new filter in the Fiori List Report called Editing Status.

This filter was not created manually in the Metadata Extension.

It was generated automatically by Fiori Elements for the draft-enabled application.

It helps users filter records according to their draft or editing state.

An important distinction is that Editing Status is different from our custom Student Status field.

  • Student Status: NEW or APPROVED, representing business approval.

  • Editing Status: Represents the draft or editing state of the record.

Key Learning

Draft Handling provides a more flexible user experience by allowing unfinished changes to be stored separately from active data.

It also demonstrates one of the major advantages of RAP: complex transactional behavior can be provided through the framework without building the complete draft lifecycle manually.

Final Result

After completing these enhancements, our Student Management Application now supports:

Feature Result

Selection FieldsFilter students by name and class
ValidationPrevent invalid student ages
DeterminationAutomatically set Student Status to NEW
Custom ActionApprove selected students
Draft HandlingKeep unfinished changes and resume later

Key Takeaways

This project helped me understand the difference between several important RAP concepts.

Validation vs. Determination

A Validation checks the consistency of data and can reject invalid changes.

A Determination automatically performs business logic when its trigger conditions are met.

Action vs. Standard CRUD

Create, Update, and Delete are standard operations, while Actions allow us to implement custom business processes such as Approve Student.

Draft vs. Active Data

Draft instances hold unfinished changes, while active instances represent the final persisted business data.

RAP Backend vs. Fiori Elements

RAP handles the transactional business logic, while Fiori Elements can generate much of the application interface based on metadata and exposed behavior.

This significantly reduces the amount of custom frontend code needed for standard business applications.

Conclusion

Enhancing my first SAP RAP application was another valuable step in my learning journey.

What started as a basic Student Management CRUD application now includes business validations, automatic status assignment, custom approval actions, and draft capabilities.

Working through these features helped me better understand how RAP handles business logic, transactional processing, and integration with SAP Fiori Elements.

References

SAP Help Portal — ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model:

https://help.sap.com/docs/abap-cloud/abap-rap

Note: This is a learning application. The authorization implementation from Part 1 is simplified for demonstration purposes and should be replaced with proper business authorization checks in production scenarios.

entry.title: GRC Tuesdays: Govern Every Identity, Human and AI, Through One Intelligent Layer
entry.content:
New SAP Business AI capability helps security and compliance teams govern, investigate, and manage both human and AI identities through a unified experience.

For the first time, many organizations must govern identities that are not human but can still access data, execute tasks, and make decisions.

The rise of AI agents is reshaping the enterprise workforce. These digital actors are streamlining operations, analysing vast amounts of information, and contributing directly to business performance. However, enterprise security architectures were designed for a world where identities belonged primarily to people. That reality has changed. Non-human identities, such as AI agents, service accounts, and automated processes, now significantly exceed human identities in many organizations, reaching ratios of up to 45 to 1 according to the Cloud Security Alliance. This shift demands a new approach to identity security, governance, and risk management.

As organizations embrace this new wave of automation, they face a challenge that traditional governance models were not designed to address: how do you govern identities that act on behalf of humans, but may operate independently across business systems?

The question for security and business leaders is no longer simply: Who has access? It is increasingly: How do we govern every identity, human and AI, with the same level of control, transparency, and accountability?

 

When authorized activity becomes a risk

 

Consider a scenario where an AI agent is operating on behalf of a business user.

The agent inherits permissions associated with its owner and begins executing tasks across business applications. No account has been compromised. No system has been breached. The activity is technically authorized.

However, a temporary access assignment that should have been removed remains in place. As a result, the AI agent can perform actions beyond what is required for its intended purpose.

Identifying the root cause requires more than understanding what happened. It requires understanding why it was possible.

This is where traditional approaches often fall short. Access governance and security monitoring frequently operate in separate processes, supported by different teams and systems. Yet as AI agents become active participants in business processes, organizations need these disciplines to work together.

Governance determines whether access should exist, detection reveals what happened with that access. Organizations need both perspectives to effectively manage risk in the age of AI.

 

The next evolution of identity governance

 

Most organizations have invested significantly in identity governance, access controls, and threat detection capabilities. These solutions answer critical questions:

  • Who has access to business-critical systems and data?
  • Does that access align with policy and compliance requirements?
  • Are there indicators of suspicious activity?
  • How quickly can teams investigate and respond?

But the rise of AI agents is changing the conversation.

Security and governance leaders need a connected view that spans the entire lifecycle of identity-related risk. They need visibility into how access is granted, how it is used, and how to respond when risks emerge.

Most importantly, they need a unified approach to governing both human and non-human identities.

 

Introducing the Access Governance and Security Assistant

 

Recently announced at SAP Connect 2026 in Las Vegas, the Access Governance and Security Assistant is SAP's agentic AI capability built to close these gaps. Designed to govern every identity through one intelligent layer.

It brings together access governance, security monitoring, investigation support, and remediation workflows into a unified conversational experience.

This Agentic Assistant is designed to help organizations enforce least-privilege access across human, non-human, and AI identities. By combining governance and security insights, it helps identify segregation-of-duties risks, streamline access reviews, monitor privileged activities, and detect anomalous behaviour using SAP-specific context. This unified approach strengthens compliance, reduces risk, and supports continuous, audit-ready oversight.

Rather than forcing teams to navigate multiple systems and manually correlate information, the Access Governance and Security Assistant helps security and compliance teams quickly understand risks, assess their impact, and act decisively.

Its capabilities span three key areas:

 

From insight to action

 

Returning to the earlier example, the Access Governance and Security Assistant can help connect an AI agent's activity with the inherited access permissions that enabled it.

Security and governance teams can quickly understand the underlying cause, launch a targeted investigation, and initiate corrective actions that remove unnecessary access while preserving legitimate business privileges.

Watch this vision demo illustrating how the Assistant could help connect SAP Enterprise Threat Detection with SAP Cloud Identity Access Governance to investigate and contain a suspicious AI agent incident - from the first alert to targeted access revocation - in minutes rather than weeks. This demo illustrates a forward-looking scenario, including cross-system risk signals and coordinated response actions that are currently under development:

Video URL: https://share.synthesia.io/0672b980-895a-45dc-ac7c-0fce9f3e6bb5

 

Business outcomes that matter

 

As organizations accelerate AI adoption, success depends on more than innovation alone. It requires trust, visibility, and governance.

Together, this leads to tangible results:

  • Up to 60% reduction in manual effort for access request reviews
  • 60–80% fewer open SoD violations following AI-assisted certification
  • 86% reduction in time to analyse and resolve security incidents

 

Preparing for the future of identity

 

The rise of AI agents represents one of the most significant shifts in enterprise technology in decades.

The future of identity governance is not about managing human identities separately from AI identities. It is about governing all identities through a single, intelligent framework that provides visibility, accountability, and control across the enterprise.

With the Access Governance and Security Assistant, organizations can connect governance and security into one continuous process and help ensure that every identity, human and AI, operates with the right access, at the right time, for the right purpose.

 

Learn More

 

To learn more about the Access Governance and Security Assistant and discover how your organization can govern every identity through one intelligent layer, visit the dedicated portal page: Autonomous Finance - Access Governance and Security Assistant

entry.title: Integrating Okta with SAP Cloud Identity Services Using a Custom SCIM 2.0 Adapter on SAP BTP
entry.content:
Introduction

Recently, I was working on an identity provisioning requirement where we needed to integrate Okta with SAP Cloud Identity Services (CIS).

The idea was simple: Okta would be the source of users and groups, and SAP Identity Provisioning (IPS) would take care of provisioning those identities into SAP Cloud Identity Services.

However, during the initial analysis, we came across an authentication challenge.

The Okta environment was configured to use OAuth 2.0 with private_key_jwt authentication for accessing its Management APIs. We needed a way for SAP IPS to retrieve users and groups while supporting this authentication mechanism.

After exploring the available options, I decided to build a small adapter using Node.js and host it on SAP BTP Cloud Foundry.

The approach worked, and I thought it would be useful to share how I built it, the architecture behind it, and a few things I learned along the way.

1. Why Did I Need a Custom Connector?

SAP Cloud Identity Services provides various options for integrating identity sources and target systems.

For this particular requirement, we wanted to use a generic SCIM 2.0 source in IPS.

The challenge was that Okta's native Management APIs use a different API structure, and our authentication requirement involved OAuth 2.0 with a signed JWT client assertion.

I wanted to avoid using long-lived Okta API tokens and keep the authentication mechanism aligned with the existing security requirements.

So, instead of trying to make IPS communicate directly with the Okta Management APIs, I introduced a small integration layer.

The idea was to let IPS communicate with a standard SCIM 2.0 endpoint while the adapter handled everything specific to Okta.

This meant I could manage authentication, API calls, and data transformations in one place without making the IPS configuration overly complicated.

2. How the Integration Works

The overall architecture is fairly straightforward.

 

Here's what happens when IPS runs a provisioning job:

  1. IPS sends a request to the SCIM endpoint hosted on SAP BTP.

  2. The Node.js application authenticates the incoming request.

  3. The adapter obtains an OAuth access token from Okta if needed.

  4. It calls the Okta APIs to retrieve users or groups.

  5. The retrieved data is converted into SCIM 2.0 format.

  6. IPS receives the response and continues with its standard provisioning process.

One thing I liked about this design was that IPS didn't need to know anything about Okta's authentication mechanism.

As far as IPS was concerned, it was communicating with a SCIM-compatible source.

3. Setting Up Authentication with Okta

This was probably the most interesting part of the implementation.

For the Okta connection, I used OAuth 2.0 client credentials with private_key_jwt authentication.

Instead of passing a client secret, the application creates a JWT assertion signed with an RSA private key.

Okta validates the assertion and issues an access token, which the adapter then uses to access the Management APIs.

For this integration, the required scopes were:

okta.users.read
okta.groups.read

The token request goes to:

POST https://{okta-domain}/oauth2/v1/token

With parameters similar to:

grant_type=client_credentials

scope=okta.users.read okta.groups.read

client_assertion_type=
urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer

client_assertion=<signed_jwt>

The Okta service application also needs the appropriate administrative permissions to read the required identity resources.

Once the access token is available, the application can call the Okta APIs.

For example, to retrieve users:

GET https://{okta-domain}/api/v1/users
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

And for groups:

GET https://{okta-domain}/api/v1/groups
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

I kept the Okta authentication logic inside the Node.js application. This way, IPS only needs its own credentials to access the SCIM service.

It also makes troubleshooting easier because the Okta authentication and IPS authentication can be checked independently.

4. Building the SCIM Adapter with Node.js

For development, I used Node.js with Express.

The application essentially acts as a translator between Okta's Management APIs and the SCIM 2.0 interface expected by IPS.

The main endpoints are:

GET /scim/v2/Users

GET /scim/v2/Groups

GET /scim/v2/Users/{id}

GET /scim/v2/Groups/{id}

I also considered standard SCIM discovery endpoints, which allow clients to understand the capabilities and schemas supported by a SCIM service.

Mapping Okta Users to SCIM

Okta returns user information in its own JSON structure.

For example:

{
  "id": "00u123456",
  "status": "ACTIVE",
  "profile": {
    "login": "john.doe@example.com",
    "firstName": "John",
    "lastName": "Doe",
    "email": "john.doe@example.com"
  }
}

But IPS expects the response to follow the SCIM schema.

So, the adapter maps the Okta attributes into something like this:

{
  "schemas": [
    "urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:core:2.0:User"
  ],
  "id": "00u123456",
  "userName": "john.doe@example.com",
  "active": true,
  "name": {
    "givenName": "John",
    "familyName": "Doe"
  },
  "emails": [
    {
      "value": "john.doe@example.com",
      "primary": true
    }
  ]
}

These are sample payloads to illustrate the mapping.

The same concept applies to groups, where the adapter maps Okta group information and memberships into the corresponding SCIM attributes.

Another thing to consider is pagination.

Okta uses cursor-based pagination for its APIs, whereas SCIM commonly uses startIndex and count.

For example:

GET /scim/v2/Users?startIndex=1&count=100

The adapter needs to handle this difference so that IPS can retrieve the required records correctly.

For larger environments, pagination becomes particularly important, along with filtering, error handling, and API rate limits.

5. Deploying the Application on SAP BTP Cloud Foundry

Once the basic adapter was ready, the next step was to deploy it.

Since I was already working in the SAP BTP ecosystem, Cloud Foundry was a natural choice.

There was no need to provision a separate server or introduce additional infrastructure.

I used a standard Node.js application structure with a Cloud Foundry manifest.

An example manifest.yml looks like this:

applications:
  - name: okta-cis-scim-adapter
    memory: 256M
    disk_quota: 512M
    buildpacks:
      - nodejs_buildpack

Deployment was done using the Cloud Foundry CLI:

cf login
cf target -o <org> -s <space>
cf push

After deployment, the application was accessible through its Cloud Foundry route.

The Okta domain, OAuth client ID, signing key and other configuration values are supplied to the application through environment-specific configuration.

For production, I would recommend using a secure secrets-management approach instead of storing private keys or credentials directly in source code.

6. Connecting SAP Identity Provisioning to the Adapter

With the application running on BTP, I moved to the SAP Cloud Identity Services side.

I created a source system in SAP Identity Provisioning using the generic SCIM system connector.

The important part was configuring the source to point to the Cloud Foundry application instead of the Okta API.

An example configuration is shown below:

Property Value

Source SystemSCIM System
URLhttps://<btp-app-route>/scim/v2
AuthenticationBasicAuthentication
Proxy TypeInternet
ResourcesUsers and Groups

The adapter was configured to accept authenticated SCIM requests, and the corresponding credentials were maintained in IPS.

From there, IPS could call the adapter, retrieve the SCIM-formatted identity data, and process it using the configured transformations and target system.

The advantage here was that the provisioning logic remained within IPS, while the adapter took care of communicating with Okta.

7. A Small Issue I Faced During Testing

Of course, the first test didn't go entirely as planned.

When I initially tested the connection from IPS, I received an HTTP 401 error.

The request was reaching the application, but the adapter was rejecting it.

Initially, I was checking the Okta OAuth configuration, but the issue turned out to be on the incoming SCIM authentication side.

After reviewing the Basic Authentication configuration and correcting the credentials, the connection worked.

This was a useful reminder that there are two different authentication layers in this setup:

IPS to the SCIM adapter: Basic Authentication over HTTPS.

SCIM adapter to Okta: OAuth 2.0 with private_key_jwt.

Once the first connection was working, I was able to validate that IPS could communicate with the deployed adapter.

The next important areas for testing in a production deployment are user and group mapping, pagination, membership handling, full provisioning runs, and retry behaviour.

8. What I Liked About This Approach

Looking back, there are a few reasons why I think this architecture makes sense.

First, it keeps the integration relatively simple. The adapter does one job: expose identity information from Okta through a standard SCIM interface.

Second, the authentication logic remains independent. If something changes in Okta's authentication requirements, the changes can be handled within the adapter without necessarily redesigning the IPS source.

Third, it's reusable. Although I built it for Okta, the same pattern could be used with another identity provider that exposes its own APIs.

And finally, SAP BTP Cloud Foundry makes it easy to host this kind of lightweight integration application alongside the rest of the SAP landscape.

That said, introducing a custom component also means taking responsibility for its maintenance, security, monitoring, and API compatibility. It's worth evaluating the available standard integration options before choosing a custom adapter.

9. A Few Takeaways

This was an interesting implementation because it involved more than just configuring an identity connector.

I had to work across Okta authentication, REST APIs, Node.js, SCIM 2.0, SAP BTP Cloud Foundry, and SAP Identity Provisioning.

A few things stood out:

  • Understanding the authentication flow before starting the integration saves time later.

  • Keeping authentication and data transformation separate makes the solution easier to troubleshoot.

  • SCIM 2.0 is a useful standard for reducing dependencies on provider-specific APIs.

  • Pagination and group membership mapping deserve attention from the beginning.

  • SAP BTP can be a practical platform for building small extensions when standard integration options don't fully match a requirement.

Source Code – GitHub Repository

I've also made the connector's implementation available on GitHub for anyone interested in exploring the approach or building something similar.

The repository includes the Node.js SCIM adapter, Okta OAuth authentication handling, and SAP BTP Cloud Foundry deployment configuration.

GitHub Repository: Custom Okta SCIM Adapter for SAP Cloud Identity Services

Feel free to explore the implementation, suggest improvements, or contribute.

Conclusion

What started as an Okta-to-SAP identity provisioning requirement eventually turned into a small but useful integration project.

By building a Node.js-based SCIM adapter and deploying it on SAP BTP Cloud Foundry, I was able to bridge the authentication and API differences between Okta and SAP Identity Provisioning.

The adapter is not intended to replace standard SAP identity connectors. It's an additional option for scenarios where specific authentication or API requirements call for a custom integration layer.

I wanted to share this experience because similar challenges can come up when integrating SAP Cloud Identity Services with different enterprise identity platforms.

Hopefully, this provides a useful starting point for anyone working on something similar.

Thanks for reading! Feel free to share your thoughts or experiences with custom identity integrations in the comments.

 

Note: This article describes a custom integration approach. The example configuration and JSON payloads are illustrative and should be validated against the actual implementation before production use.

entry.title: ALMathon 2026 - abat QA Cockpit: Ensure code quality in your Cloud ALM projects
entry.content:
Overview

The QA-Cockpit is an extension to SAP Cloud ALM that closes a gap in Cloud ALM around structured quality assurance for features before they go live.

In recent years quality assurance in SAP development has become increasingly important. It is essential to ensure aspects such as maintainability, a „Clean Core“ and security. For this reason, some customers have customized the Solution Manager for instance by implementing own statuses and individual checks. However, this is not possible with Cloud ALM, as the statuses and check routines are predefined. During ALMathon 2026, we bridged this gap by developing a comprehensive extension and adding features that are indispensable for modern development processes.

Developed during the SAP ALMathon

As part of the ALMathon, our litte team from the abat AG contributed a fully working prototype of the QA-Cockpit. The solution was ideated, designed and implemented during the hackathon, showing how SAP Cloud ALM can be extended with a dedicated quality-assurance layer that fits natively into the Cloud ALM experience

Why does the world need a QA-Cockpit?

SAP Cloud ALM gives teams strong feature and requirement management, but it does not provide a structured gate for quality sign-off, before a feature is released for testing or production. The situation quickly becomes complicated, when that feature involves several transports and transport objects that a QA reviewer must evaluate individually. The QA-Cockpit fills this gap by turning every Cloud ALM feature into a trackable „QA-Case“ with its own status, owner and audit trail. You can also view and click on the feature, project and requirement to which it belongs. By providing an AI review for the reviewer and the developer, even mandatory peer-reviews can be replaced. Additionally, the reviewer gains an overview that facilitates their work.

Challenges addressed

  • Transports, objects, check results and source code are stored in different systems, so the teams had to jump between systems to make their review.
  • The decisions (such as status changes and justifications) were not documented.
  • It was difficult to track who approved what and why.

Key features

  • Feature synchronisation: Each relevant feature automatically becomes a QA-Case and receives a clickable reference in Cloud ALM, allowing you to easily navigate to the QA-Cockpit
  • Transports, transport objects & transport checks: All technical artifacts underlying a feature are visible in one place, with automated checks surfaced directly in the QA-Case
  • AI review: An AI-generated review supports the reviewer by highlighting findings and summarizing the source code
  • Decision workflow: The actions „Approve“, „Reject“, „Not Relevant“ and „Assign“ move a QA-Case through a clearly defined status lifecycle
  • Comments & collaboration: Requester and reviewer can discuss directly in the QA-Case, with the entire history documented alongside
  • Audit log: Every status change and action is recorded for traceability
  • Native Cloud ALM look & feel: The application is based on SAP Fiori Elements and visually aligned with the Cloud ALM shell. This makes it appear as an integral part of Cloud ALM rather than a separate tool
  • Multilingual: The UI is available in English and German, switchable at any time

 

Inside QA-Cockpit

Overview QA-Cases

Below you can see a list of QA-cases, which were derived by the single features. This list can be used as backlog. A QA Team could use it to dispatch the cases in a regulary appointment.

Detailed view of QA-Case

If you click on a single case, wesee multiple details, which are linked to the corresponding QA entities as project, feature or requirement.

 

 

Architecture highlights

The architecture of QA-Cockpit leverages the following key components:

  • SAP Cloud Application Programming Model (CAP): Powers the backend OData V4 service, the QA Case data model, and the decision/workflow actions.
  • SAP Fiori Elements (SAPUI5): Provides the List Report and Object Page UI for reviewing QA-Cases, transports, and AI findings.
  • SAP Cloud ALM APIs: Used to automatically synchronize features, transports, and transport objects into the QA-Cockpit.
  • AI review: Generates the pre-review findings shown on each QA-Case to support the reviewer.

What’s next

The QA-Cockpit started as a ALMathon build, but we see it as a starting point rather than a finished product, so we’re looking forward to testing it and getting better every day. We‘d love to hear from other SAP Cloud ALM  users for feedback, questions and collaboration opportunities. And if you want to know more about our product, please send us a message

Conclusion

Cloud ALM is a very good solution, which enables to implement requirements and enhance the standard solutions. Unfortunately, it's not possible to ensure code quality inside of the standard process. The QA-Cockpit fills this gap by providing many different checks as well to ensure approvals by quality managers.

The cockpit will optimize the development process including quality instead of only tracking implementation.
